text: The same result, told to a hiring manager, a product team, or a general audience, needs a genuinely different telling — not a dumbed-down version of the technical talk, but a different structure built around what a non-specialist actually needs to follow and trust.

This lesson covers why simplifying the technical talk is the wrong mental model, how to translate quantum-specific jargon into accurate, non-misleading plain language, a structure for a non-specialist talk that still represents limitations honestly, and how to avoid overselling to an audience that can't independently check your claims.

Zero-noise extrapolation becomes a correction technique that deliberately adds controlled extra noise, measures how the result degrades, and uses that pattern to estimate what the result would have been with no noise at all. A GHZ state becomes a standard test case whose correct answer is known in advance, useful for measuring how much noise affects a device. Shots become repeated measurements, like flipping a coin many times instead of once. Resist translating in a way that overstates certainty — the hardware's imperfections are partly predictable and partly correctable, not simply 'a mistake.'

A structure for this audience: the real-world stakes in one sentence, a concrete visualizable analogy for the core concept, what you did in plain language without circuit diagrams, what you found with the actual numbers translated into accessible framing like percentages, honest caveats stated in plain language, and one closing sentence connecting back to the stakes.

A worked plain-language version: quantum computers today are noisy, they make mistakes. We tested a correction technique on a standard test circuit, run on real hardware, at two sizes. It cut the number of wrong measurements by about two-thirds at the smaller size, and by a bit less at the larger size — consistent with correction getting harder as circuits grow. We only tested two sizes on one device, so we can't yet say how this pattern holds as quantum computers get bigger, but it's a concrete, measured data point toward understanding that question.
